system_map.overview: The CAS runner is a CLI-driven tool that manages continuous architecture governance. It orchestrates actions, evaluates health, checks compliance, and merges agent configurations. The system is structured into distinct layers: presentation (CLI), application (runner, services), domain (Pydantic models), and infrastructure (LLM clients, file system integration).

layers.name: Presentation Layer
layers.purpose: Provide a command-line interface for user interaction and orchestrate top-level workflows.

layers.name: Application Layer
layers.purpose: Encapsulate use-case logic: governance actions, compliance checks, health calculation, and evaluation orchestration.

containers.name: CLI Entry Point
containers.purpose: Parses commands and delegates to runner or services.

containers.purpose: Executes flows by coordinating steps and services.

containers.name: Governance Action Engine
containers.purpose: Manages state transitions for governance actions via a registry.

containers.name: Compliance Engine
containers.purpose: Checks compliance rules against governance inventory.

containers.purpose: Merges agent-related configuration files (non-agentic structural merge).

containers.name: LLM Clients
containers.purpose: Provide abstraction over LLM providers (LiteLLM and Mock).

containers.name: Skill Evaluation Models
containers.purpose: Define structured models for skill evaluation cases and results.

patterns.name: Pydantic Domain Entity Modeling
patterns.summary: Domain entities are defined as Pydantic models, providing validation, serialization, and type safety.
patterns.intent: To represent complex governance and evaluation concepts with structured, validated data objects.
patterns.context: The system deals with governance inventory, actions, compliance findings, and skill evaluation results, all requiring strict schemas for consistency.
forces: Need for data integrity across different subsystems.
Desire for easy serialization to JSON/YAML for persistence.
Flexibility to extend models with new fields.
patterns.solution: Define all domain objects as Pydantic BaseModel subclasses, using type hints and validators to enforce invariants. For example, GovernanceAction, ComplianceFinding, SkillEvalResult are models in governance/models.py and skills/models.py.
implementation_signals: Models contain typed fields with default values.
Use of Pydantic decorators and validators for constraints.
Models are imported across multiple layers.

benefits: Type safety, validation, and serialization out-of-the-box.
Models can be combined and reused across services.
costs: Possible over-validation overhead for large datasets.
failure_modes: If validation rules become too complex, models become hard to maintain.

patterns.reuse_notes: Applies to any new domain concept introduced in the system.

extraction_metadata.basis: File structure and symbol names indicate consistent use of Pydantic models in domain layer.

patterns.name: LLM Client Adapter Pattern
patterns.summary: LLM provider interactions are abstracted behind a client interface, with concrete implementations for real and mock providers.
patterns.intent: To decouple higher layers from specific LLM providers, enabling swapping or testing.
patterns.context: The system needs to call LLMs for various tasks but should remain provider-agnostic and testable.
forces: Need to support multiple LLM providers (LiteLLM, Azure, etc.).
Testing requires deterministic mock responses.
Configuration should allow selecting implementation at runtime.
patterns.solution: Define a common interface (possibly implicit via duck typing) for LLM clients. LiteLLMClient wraps litellm, while MockLLMClient returns canned responses. Both are used interchangeably in higher-level code.
implementation_signals: Separate module for LLM clients.
Classes with similar method signatures.
Presence of a mock implementation for tests.

benefits: Provider isolation, easy testing, clean dependency inversion.
failure_modes: If interface is not explicit, implementations may drift.

patterns.reuse_notes: Adopt for any external service that may vary.

extraction_metadata.basis: Two client implementations in same package, likely shared interface.

patterns.name: Service Layer for Governance Actions
patterns.summary: Business operations for governance actions are encapsulated in a service class, separating use-case logic from presentation and data access.
patterns.intent: To provide a single entry point for governance-related operations, reducing duplication and centralizing rules.
patterns.context: Governance actions require coordination of state transitions, validation, and persistence. A service layer centralizes these responsibilities.
forces: Avoid scattering business logic across CLI and runners.
Maintain transactional integrity for action lifecycle.
Enable unit testing of business rules.
patterns.solution: Create GovernanceActionService that exposes methods to execute and transition governance actions, delegating state changes to GovernanceActionEngine and persistence to repositories.
implementation_signals: Service class name ending in 'Service'.
Methods orchestrate multiple dependencies.
Used by higher-level orchestrators like FlowRunner.

benefits: Centralized transaction management, easier testing, clear separation of concerns.
costs: Service can become a facade if too many responsibilities.
failure_modes: Business rules may leak into callers if service becomes too generic.

patterns.reuse_notes: Use for any complex aggregate operation in the system.

extraction_metadata.basis: Presence of dedicated service class alongside engine and models.

patterns.name: Transition Registry State Machine
patterns.summary: Governance actions have a defined set of states and allowed transitions, enforced via a transition registry.
patterns.intent: To ensure that governance actions only move to valid next states, preventing inconsistent workflows.
patterns.context: Governance actions (e.g., approve, reject, escalate) follow a lifecycle with constraints.
forces: State transitions must be validated to avoid invalid operations.
New states/transitions should be added without modifying core logic.
Transparency of allowed transitions is needed.
patterns.solution: Implement a TransitionRegistry that maps current state to allowed future states. GovernanceActionEngine consults this registry during state changes.
implementation_signals: A registry class with mapping data.
Engine methods check registry before transition.
Use of enums for states.

benefits: Centralized validation, easy to audit, extensible via registry updates.
costs: Overhead of registry lookup for each transition.
failure_modes: Registry can become inconsistent if not maintained.

patterns.reuse_notes: Useful for any stateful entity in the domain.

extraction_metadata.basis: Explicit TransitionRegistry class in governance engine.

patterns.name: Health Calculation as Pure Function
patterns.summary: Health status is computed via a pure function that takes metrics and returns a status and reasons.
patterns.intent: To keep health assessment deterministic and testable, separate from UI and persistence.
patterns.context: The dashboard requires consistent health evaluation across different data sources.
forces: Health logic should be simple and easy to test.
Reasons must be human-readable.
Statuses should be predefined (e.g., healthy, degraded).
patterns.solution: Implement calculate_health(metrics) and get_health_reasons(metrics) as standalone functions, returning HealthStatus and list of reasons.
implementation_signals: Functions in a single module, not tied to a class.
Input and output are data structures.
Pure functions without side effects.

costs: May become less structured if health logic grows.
failure_modes: Logic may be duplicated if used across multiple layers.

patterns.reuse_notes: Apply to any simple transformation of metrics to status.

extraction_metadata.basis: Function names and context suggest pure computation.

patterns.name: Bootstrap Workspace Initialization
patterns.summary: A bootstrap process prepares the workspace by merging configuration files, creating symlinks, and rendering checklists.
patterns.intent: To automate environment setup and ensure consistent project structure across users.
patterns.context: The system requires specific configuration files (e.g., .claude/settings.json) and governance blocks to be present before running.
forces: Reproducible environment setup
Merging existing user configs with defaults
Cross-platform file operations
patterns.solution: The bootstrap function performs: merge_cas_governance_block, merge_claude_settings, _create_symlink_or_copy, render_onboarding_checklist, and init_workspace to set up required files and directories.
implementation_signals: A dedicated bootstrap module with multiple subroutines.
Functions for merging and file system operations.
Used at initial setup or CLI startup.

costs: Complex merging logic may be error-prone.
Tight coupling to file system and specific config formats.
failure_modes: If file paths change, bootstrap may break.

patterns.reuse_notes: Useful for any command-line tool requiring workspace initialization.

extraction_metadata.basis: Function names and typical bootstrap responsibilities.

patterns.name: Compliance Engine Dedicated Checker
patterns.summary: Compliance checking is isolated in a dedicated engine, separate from action execution and UI.
patterns.intent: To centralize rule evaluation and keep compliance logic maintainable.
patterns.context: The system needs to verify that governance inventory adheres to policies, generating findings.
forces: Rules can change independently of action flows.
Compliance results need to be reported clearly.
Engine should be reusable across different entry points.
patterns.solution: Implement ComplianceEngine class that takes inventory data and returns compliance findings.
implementation_signals: Class named ComplianceEngine.
Methods for evaluating and generating findings.
Used by services or runners.

benefits: Separation of concerns, easier to test compliance rules.
costs: May become a god object if too many rules.
failure_modes: If rules are scattered, duplication may occur.

patterns.reuse_notes: Apply to any domain with complex validation rules.

extraction_metadata.basis: Class name and typical role of a compliance engine.

patterns.name: Agentic Configuration Merger
patterns.summary: Agent-specific configurations are merged with defaults using a dedicated merger class.
patterns.intent: To combine agent settings from multiple sources without overwriting user customizations.
patterns.context: The system needs to inject governance blocks into agent configuration files (e.g., .claude/settings.json) while preserving user edits.
forces: Preserve user-specific settings.
Handle JSON/YAML merging.
Provide deterministic results.
patterns.solution: AgenticMerger (in agentic_merger.py) implements merging logic for agent configuration files, used by bootstrap.
implementation_signals: Class named 'AgenticMerger' with merge methods.
Used in bootstrap or CLI setup.

benefits: Centralized merging logic, reuse across workflows.
failure_modes: If merge rules are not clear, user configs may be lost.

patterns.reuse_notes: Use for any configuration file that requires merging defaults with user overrides.

extraction_metadata.basis: Class name and typical usage in bootstrap.

anti_patterns.name: God Object Risk in Domain Models
symptoms: Large number of models in a single module (governance/models.py) may indicate violation of Single Responsibility.
Models may grow with many fields and methods.
suggested_remediation: Split models into separate modules by aggregate or feature.

anti_patterns.name: Implicit Interface for LLM Clients
symptoms: No explicit base class or Protocol for LLM clients.
Potential method signature drift between LiteLLMClient and MockLLMClient.
impact: Difficult to mock or swap clients.
suggested_remediation: Define a Protocol or ABC for LLM clients.
